title: A hymn in Bihagra
hook: inside the Bihagra ballad, a salok headed with Mardana's name talks about wine

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Bihagra, and your line was night longing. What tender name did you give your own heart? A new week begins, still at night. Day one thousand seventy-nine.

A wine jar, a cup, and someone drinking far too much. Not the picture one might expect inside a holy book's night raga. But there it is, in the ballad of Bihagra in the Guru Granth Sahib. Between the ballad's stanzas sit short verses called saloks, and some of them carry a heading with a name: Mardana, Guru Nanak's companion, the rabab player who traveled with him. Today: a hymn in Bihagra.
screen: `A WINE JAR AND A CUP.` → `A SALOK HEADED MARDANA.` → `INSIDE THE NIGHT BALLAD.`

segments.voice: The ballad is the Var of Bihagra, with stanzas by Guru Ram Das and saloks set between them. One salok, headed Mardana, paints the scene, given here in plain English. This dark age is the wine jar. Desire is the wine. The mind is the one drinking. Anger is the cup, filled with attachment, and pride is the one pouring. Anyone who's watched someone lose a night to drinking knows the picture: the cup keeps getting filled, and the drinker keeps reaching. The salok says the mind does the same with desire. Then it turns the picture around. Make the body the still, it says, and from it draw a different drink, one that runs like nectar. In the company of the holy, the cup becomes loving attention, filled with that nectar, and drinking it cuts the faults away. The night raga fits. Bihagra is the raga of separation, and here the longing that might pour itself into the wrong cup is turned toward God. Now, who wrote it? The heading names Mardana along with the mark the Granth uses for Guru Nanak. Sikh readers take that in more than one way. Some Sikh scholars read these saloks as Guru Nanak's own words, spoken to Mardana or about him. Others read the heading as giving the words to Mardana himself. The Granth doesn't stop to settle it, and neither do we. Either way, a companion's name stands on the page beside the Guru's, in a ballad sung at night. Today's line: longing at night. The longing doesn't vanish. It finds its proper cup.
screen: `THE DARK AGE IS THE WINE JAR.` · `DESIRE THE WINE, THE MIND THE DRINKER.` · `A DIFFERENT CUP: LOVING ATTENTION.` · `MARDANA'S NAME ON THE PAGE.` · then, large: `LONGING AT NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice what your longing reaches for. Sit, and let your breath slow. Think of the last thing you reached for late at night, scrolling, snacking, one more episode, one more glass. No judgment. Just see the reach. Now ask what the reach was really for: rest, company, comfort, quiet. Hold that real wish for a moment. If you pray, you can offer it with Waheguru. If you don't, simply name the wish to yourself. Tonight, play one Bihagra shabad as the last thing before sleep. The bell holds the time.

A hymn in Bihagra. A salok in the Bihagra ballad, headed with Mardana's name, where desire is the wine and the mind the drinker, until loving attention becomes the cup and nectar the drink. Today's word.
Your line: longing at night. Tonight, when the late reach for something comes, stop once and ask what you're really thirsty for. Day one thousand seventy-nine.

howItsDone: The Var of Bihagra is sung in kirtan with its saloks, and Sikh scholars discuss the saloks headed with Mardana's name, reading them either as Guru Nanak's words addressed to Mardana or as Mardana's own.

notes: The salok headed 'Mardana 1' (Ang 553) is paraphrased: the dark age (Kalyug) as the wine-vessel, desire as wine, the mind as drinker, anger as the cup filled with pride; then a better 'wine' of the Word and virtue. Please confirm the paraphrase, especially the second half, which is kept general on purpose.
Authorship: presented as two readings without ranking (Guru Nanak's words addressed to Mardana; Mardana's own).
'A few of them carry a heading with Mardana's name' (the outline says 'some'); please confirm the count is fairly described.
'Stanzas by Guru Ram Das' for the Bihagra Var pauris; please confirm, and confirm the Ang range.

Editor pass: the salok reads krodh katori mohi bhari, peelaava ahankaar (anger the cup, filled with attachment; ego the server), so 'anger is the cup, filled by pride' was corrected in voice and games. The vague 'drink made from the Word and the virtues' now follows the salok's own second half (kaaia laahan, aap mad, amrit tis ki dhaar; satsangat; liv katori amrit bhari, pee pee katah bikaar), paraphrased; please confirm.
